note: Seed entries for in-UI tooltips and the Learn panel. Keep definitions short, accurate, and non-mystical. Expand as needed. Each term should be tappable wherever it first appears.

terms.short: The 'Book of Changes' — one of the oldest texts in the world, used as a wisdom and divinatory text for over 3,000 years.
terms.long: A foundational Chinese classic built on 64 six-line figures (hexagrams). Originally a divination manual of the early Zhou period, it later accreted layers of philosophical commentary and was absorbed into both Daoist and Confucian traditions.

terms.short: A solid, unbroken line (⚊). Associated with the active, firm, light aspect.
terms.long: One of the two line types. In casting it appears as 'young yang' (7, stable) or 'old yang' (9, moving).

terms.short: A broken line (⚋). Associated with the receptive, yielding, dark aspect.
terms.long: One of the two line types. In casting it appears as 'young yin' (8, stable) or 'old yin' (6, moving). Yin and yang are complementary, not opposed in value.

terms.short: A line at its extreme (old yin 6 or old yang 9) that is about to turn into its opposite.
terms.long: Moving lines carry special commentary and transform the primary hexagram into a second, 'relating' hexagram — showing where the situation is tending. Stable lines (7, 8) do not change.

terms.short: A figure of three lines. There are eight, each tied to a natural image (Heaven, Earth, Fire, Water, Thunder, Wind, Mountain, Lake).
terms.long: Two trigrams stack to form a hexagram. The lower trigram is read as the inner/near aspect, the upper as the outer/far. Each trigram also carries a family role and an attribute.

terms.short: A figure of six lines — the unit you consult. There are 64, numbered in the King Wen sequence.
terms.long: Built from two trigrams. Each hexagram has a name, an image, a Judgment, and line-by-line texts. The 64 cover a wide range of human situations.

terms.short: The core oracle text for a hexagram as a whole.
terms.long: A terse statement on the overall situation the hexagram describes, followed in tradition by commentary. Presented here in the translation you've selected.

terms.short: A reflection pairing the hexagram's natural symbolism with how the 'superior person' acts in response.
terms.long: Known as the Da Xiang ('Great Image'). It reads the two trigrams as natural phenomena and draws an ethical or practical orientation from them.

terms.short: The second hexagram formed when moving lines flip to their opposites.
terms.long: It does not predict a fixed outcome; it indicates the direction in which the present situation is tending. A reading with no moving lines has no relating hexagram.

terms.short: The 'hidden' trigrams formed by the inner lines (2-3-4 and 3-4-5) of a hexagram.
terms.long: An advanced reading device: the nuclear trigrams reveal an inner tendency within the hexagram. Shown here only when you opt into the advanced view.

terms.short: The oldest casting method: dividing and counting 50 dried stalks through several rounds per line.
terms.long: Slow and meditative. Its line outcomes are deliberately unequal — old yang and old yin are rarer than under coins — which gives moving lines particular weight. This app can use the authentic asymmetric odds or a simplified equal-style model (your choice in Settings).

terms.short: A faster method: toss three coins six times; the mix of heads and tails gives each line.
terms.long: More common today. Each line is equally likely to be moving yin or moving yang (1/8 each), unlike the yarrow method's asymmetry.

terms.short: The traditional 1–64 ordering of the hexagrams used throughout this app.
terms.long: Attributed by tradition to King Wen of Zhou. It is the standard ordering in which the hexagrams and their texts are arranged.
